Leeward means on the side that is sheltered from the wind — or more simply, facing away from the wind.

To truly understand this word, you first need to picture wind blowing in one direction. The wind always comes from one side and blows toward another. Those two sides have names:

  • The side the wind is hitting directly (exposed, facing the wind) → windward
  • The side the wind is blowing toward (sheltered, facing away from the wind) → leeward

So leeward always describes the protected, downwind side of something.
Make It Click With a Simple Example

Imagine you're standing outside on a windy day, and there's a large wall next to you. The wind is slamming into one face of the wall.

  • The face of the wall getting hit by the wind = the windward face.
  • The other face of the wall — the calm, sheltered side where you're hiding — = the leeward face.

You, standing in that calm pocket of air, are on the leeward side of the wall.

That's the exact logic of the word, applied everywhere it's used.
Where You'll See This Word Used

1. On Ships and in Sailing

This is where the word is most at home. A ship has two sides at all times — one facing the wind and one facing away from it.

  • The leeward side of a ship is the side facing away from the wind. It's calmer, more protected, and less exposed to spray and gusts. Sailors historically preferred to work or stand on the leeward side.
  • If a ship is said to be sailing in a leeward direction, it means it's sailing away from the wind — letting the wind push it along from behind, rather than fighting into it.

2. In Geography and Weather (Mountains)

This is one of the most important real-world uses of the word.

When wind blows toward a mountain, it hits one side — the windward side — rises up over it, cools, and releases rain or snow. By the time that air spills over the top and comes down the other side, it has lost most of its moisture.

  • The leeward side of a mountain is the dry, sheltered side facing away from the wind. It often sits in what's called a rain shadow — a dry zone that gets very little rainfall because the mountain blocks the moisture-carrying winds.

A real-world example: The Sierra Nevada mountains in California have a lush, wet windward side (facing the Pacific winds) and a dry desert on the leeward side (the Great Basin).

3. In Place Names

"Leeward" also appears in geography as a proper name. The Leeward Islands, for instance, are a group of islands in the Caribbean. They were named "leeward" because they were on the sheltered, downwind side relative to the direction of the prevailing trade winds — compared to the Windward Islands, which faced directly into those winds.

You'll often see the shorter word lee used on its own. It means the same thing — shelter from the wind, or the sheltered side of something. So if a sailor says "get into the lee of that island," they mean "get on the sheltered side of that island, out of the wind." Leeward is simply the directional, adjective form of lee — it tells you which side or which direction.
The One Contrast That Locks It All In

WindwardFacing into the wind. Exposed. Where the wind hits first.
LeewardFacing away from the wind. Sheltered. Where the wind arrives last.
Leeward describes the side of something — a ship, a mountain, an island, a wall — that faces away from the wind and is therefore sheltered and protected from it.
